## Today...

**One predictor was never the plan.**

- Why a second predictor changes the first one's meaning
- "Holding constant" — what it actually does
- A slope that **flips sign** when we add the right variable
- Did the new predictor earn its place? (Model Builder + Model Comparisons)
- *b* or *β*: which one do you report?
- When predictors step on each other (collinearity)

::: callout-note
This is the **JAMOVI** version of Week 8. Same models, same numbers, same interpretations — all point-and-click. The R version is [here](lec-08_multiple-reg.html).
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Where we have been

| Week | Model | What was new |
|------|-------|--------------|
| 5 | $Y = b_0 + b_1X$ | one continuous predictor (**Covariates**) |
| 6 | $Y = b_0 + b_1D$ | the predictor can be a group (**Factors**) |
| 7 | $SS_{total} = SS_{model} + SS_{res}$ | how well the line fits |

. . .

Everything so far has been **one predictor at a time**. That is almost never the model you want.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The only equation we need

$$Y_i = b_0 + b_1X_{1i} + b_2X_{2i} + \dots + b_kX_{ki} + e_i$$

::: incremental
- $b_0$ — predicted $Y$ when **every** predictor is 0
- $b_1$ — change in $Y$ per 1-unit change in $X_1$, **holding the other predictors constant**
- $e_i$ — still the part we miss
:::

. . .

::: callout-important
In JAMOVI you build this model by dragging **more than one variable** into **Covariates**. That is the entire mechanical change. Everything else today is about what the numbers now *mean*.
:::

# Part 1: Why Bother?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## You have been hired by the county 🚒

The fire department wants to know what drives the **cost of a fire**.

300 fires: how many **trucks** were dispatched, how many **acres** burned, and the **damage** in thousands of dollars.

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Open the data

**☰ Menu → Open → Browse →** `fire_data.csv`

Four columns: `fire_id`, `acres`, `trucks`, `damage`. Confirm all three analysis variables are **Continuous**.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Start where we always start

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Look at it first

**Exploration → scatr → Scatterplot**

- `trucks` → **X-Axis**
- `damage` → **Y-Axis**
- **Regression Line:** Linear
:::

A clear, tight, positive cloud. More trucks, more damage.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The bivariate model

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Fit it

**Regression → Linear Regression**

- `damage` → **Dependent Variable**
- `trucks` → **Covariates**
- **Model Coefficients:** ✅ Estimate, ✅ Standard error, ✅ p-value
- **Model Fit:** ✅ R², ✅ Adjusted R², ✅ Overall model test (F test)
:::

| Predictor | *b* | *SE* | *t* | *p* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intercept | 8.84 | 3.28 | 2.70 | .007 |
| `trucks` | **12.73** | 0.51 | 24.73 | \< .001 |

*R²* = **.672**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What would you tell the county?

::: incremental
- *b* = **12.73**: each additional truck is associated with **\$12,730 more** damage
- $p$ \< .001, $R^2$ = .67 — this is not a fragile finding
:::

. . .

> "Trucks strongly predict damage. **Send fewer trucks.**"

. . .

::: callout-warning
Every number in that sentence is correct. The recommendation would get people killed.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 🧠 Side quest: draw the thing {background-color="#EFE6F7"}

Before you fit anything, sketch what you think is going on. Arrows for "causes."

- Does `trucks` → `damage`?
- Does something cause **both**?

. . .

A variable that causes both your predictor and your outcome is a **confound**. Leave it out and your slope absorbs its effect.

These sketches have a name — **Directed Acyclic Graphs** — and Dr. Haraden is about to abuse the chalkboard with one. 🧑‍🏫

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The variable we ignored

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Colour the cloud by fire size

**Exploration → scatr → Scatterplot**

- `trucks` → **X-Axis**, `damage` → **Y-Axis**
- `acres` → **Group** *(JAMOVI will bin a continuous grouping variable; alternatively make a 3-level size variable under **Data → Compute** using `IF`)*
:::

Big fires get more trucks **and** do more damage. The slope we estimated was mostly **fire size wearing a truck costume**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Put acres in the model

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ One extra drag

In the same **Linear Regression** panel, drag `acres` into **Covariates** underneath `trucks`.
:::

| Predictor | *b* | *SE* | *t* | *p* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intercept | 10.94 | 1.65 | 6.62 | \< .001 |
| `trucks` | **−2.63** | 0.58 | −4.54 | \< .001 |
| `acres` | **4.09** | 0.14 | 29.64 | \< .001 |

*R²* = **.917**, adj. *R²* = .917

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The sign flipped

::: incremental
- `trucks`: **+12.73 → −2.63**
- `acres`: +4.09 per acre
- $R^2$: .672 → **.917**
:::

. . .

Each additional truck is associated with **\$2,630 less** damage — **among fires of the same size**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What just happened

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Before**

We compared a 2-truck fire to a 9-truck fire. Those are not the same fire. One was a kitchen; one was a neighborhood.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**After**

We compare 2-truck and 3-truck fires **of the same acreage**. Now the extra truck can only help.
:::
:::::

. . .

::: callout-important
## "Holding constant" is a comparison, not a magic word

$b_1$ answers: among cases that are **identical on every other predictor in the model**, what is the difference in $Y$ per unit of $X_1$?

Identical on the predictors you *included*. Nothing else.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Omitted variables do not politely disappear

When you leave out a variable that is related to both $X$ and $Y$, its effect does not vanish — it gets **folded into** the coefficients you did estimate.

::: incremental
- Sometimes the slope is **inflated** (the trucks case)
- Sometimes it is **shrunk** (next week's tutoring example)
- Sometimes it appears out of nowhere (Lab 8's suppression)
- Sometimes **nothing moves** — and that is a finding too
:::

. . .

You cannot tell which from the output. You can only tell from **what you chose to measure**.

# Part 2: Real Data, Real Stakes

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 520 students, one survey 😵‍💫

A student-stress survey: everything rated 1–5.

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Open and rename

**☰ Menu → Open → Browse →** `student_stress.xlsx`

The column headers are full sentences (with emoji). Double-click each header and give it a short **Name**:

| Original question | Name it |
|---|---|
| Rate your sleep quality | `sleep_quality` |
| Headaches per week | `headaches` |
| Rate your academic performance | `academic_perf` |
| Rate your study load | `study_load` |
| Extracurriculars per week | `extracurricular` |
| Rate your stress levels | `stress` |

Set all six to **Continuous**.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Describe, then correlate

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Two panels

1.  **Exploration → Descriptives** — all six variables, ✅ Mean, ✅ SD, ✅ Minimum, ✅ Maximum
2.  **Regression → Correlation Matrix** — all six variables
:::

| | *r* with stress |
|---|---|
| `study_load` | **.392** |
| `sleep_quality` | **.165** |
| `extracurricular` | .052 |
| `academic_perf` | .055 |
| `headaches` | −.072 |

. . .

And the two predictors we care about barely know each other: *r*(study_load, sleep_quality) = **.065**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Model 1: study load alone

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Linear Regression

`stress` → **Dependent Variable** · `study_load` → **Covariates**
:::

| Predictor | *b* | *SE* | *t* | *p* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intercept | 1.810 | 0.123 | 14.72 | \< .001 |
| `study_load` | **0.388** | 0.040 | 9.69 | \< .001 |

*R²* = **.153**, adj. *R²* = .152, RSE = 1.251

. . .

Each 1-point increase in study load → **0.39** points more stress.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Model 2: add sleep quality

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Drag `sleep_quality` into **Covariates**
:::

| Predictor | *b* | *SE* | *t* | *p* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Intercept | 1.292 | 0.191 | 6.76 | \< .001 |
| `study_load` | **0.378** | 0.040 | 9.54 | \< .001 |
| `sleep_quality` | **0.174** | 0.050 | 3.50 | \< .001 |

. . .

| Predictor | Alone | Together |
|---|---|---|
| `study_load` | 0.388 | **0.378** |

The study-load slope moved by **0.01**. Essentially nothing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why nothing moved

A coefficient only changes when the new predictor is related to **both** the outcome and the old predictor.

::: incremental
- *r*(study_load, sleep_quality) = **.065** → the two predictors carry **separate** information
- So each one keeps the effect it had on its own
- Their contributions simply **add**
:::

. . .

::: callout-tip
"I added a predictor and the first one didn't budge" is a **real result**, and it is the common one. It means your two predictors are not competing for the same variance. Say that, instead of apologizing for it.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Interpreting Model 2 out loud

$$\widehat{Stress} = 1.29 + 0.378(StudyLoad) + 0.174(SleepQuality)$$

::: incremental
- **1.29** — predicted stress for a student who rated study load *and* sleep quality as 0. **Neither is possible** (the scale starts at 1), so this intercept is a mathematical anchor, not a person.
- **0.378** — comparing two students with the **same sleep quality**, one point more study load goes with 0.38 points more stress
- **0.174** — comparing two students with the **same study load**, one point more sleep quality goes with 0.17 points more stress
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Wait. Read that last one again. 🤨

**Better sleep quality predicts *more* stress** (*b* = +0.174, *p* \< .001), holding study load constant.

. . .

Three possibilities, and you cannot choose between them from this output:

::: incremental
1.  The item is scored **backwards** — maybe 5 means "I rate my sleep quality as a problem"
2.  The relationship is real and reflects something else (students who sleep well take on more)
3.  The survey question was ambiguous and students interpreted it inconsistently
:::

. . .

::: callout-important
This is the midterm's lesson arriving in a lecture. **Check the direction of every coefficient against what you expected.** When it disagrees, the first suspect is always scoring — not the universe.
:::

# Part 3: Did It Earn Its Place?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## JAMOVI does this better than R 🏆

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Model Builder

Inside **Linear Regression**, open the **Model Builder** section:

1.  `study_load` → **Block 1**
2.  Click **+ Add New Block**
3.  `sleep_quality` → **Block 2**

Then open **Model Comparisons** and tick **Compare models**.
:::

JAMOVI now reports both models side by side **and** the test of the difference. In R this takes a second `lm()` and an `anova()` call.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Model Fit Comparison table

| Model | *R²* | adj. *R²* | RSE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. study load | .1534 | .1517 | 1.2506 |
| 2. \+ sleep quality | **.1730** | **.1698** | **1.2372** |

**Model Comparisons:** Δ*R²* = **.0196**, *F*(1, 517) = **12.27**, *p* \< **.001**

::: incremental
- About 2% more of stress accounted for
- Adjusted $R^2$ went **up**, so the predictor paid its own df
- Typical miss shrank from 1.251 to 1.237 (on a variable with SD = 1.358)
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What that *F* actually is

The comparison test asks: *does the drop in unexplained variability exceed what one extra predictor would buy by chance?*

::: incremental
- Residual SS: 810.12 → **791.34**
- The new predictor picked up **18.78** of it
- $F$(1, 517) = **12.27**, *p* = .0005
:::

. . .

With one added predictor, this $F$ is just the square of its $t$: $3.503^2 = 12.27$. Same test, different table. ✅

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Now let's add three useless things

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Block 3

Add `extracurricular`, `headaches` and `academic_perf` together as **Block 3**.
:::

| Predictor | *b* | *p* |
|---|---|---|
| `study_load` | 0.383 | \< .001 |
| `sleep_quality` | 0.178 | \< .001 |
| `extracurricular` | −0.015 | **.697** |
| `headaches` | −0.074 | **.097** |
| `academic_perf` | −0.038 | **.483** |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Watch the two R²s diverge

| Model | *R²* | adj. *R²* | RSE |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 predictors | .1730 | .1698 | 1.2372 |
| 5 predictors | **.1779** ⬆️ | **.1699** ➡️ | 1.2371 |

::: incremental
- $R^2$ rose by .005, because **it always rises**
- Adjusted $R^2$ moved by **.0001** — three predictors bought you nothing
- RSE: unchanged to four decimals
:::

. . .

::: callout-important
Week 7's warning, now with consequences. $R^2$ cannot tell you whether a predictor belongs in the model. **Adjusted $R^2$, the model comparison, and your theory** can.
:::

# Part 4: Reporting It

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## *b* or *β*?

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Standardized estimates

**Model Coefficients → ✅ Standardized estimate**

JAMOVI adds a `Stand. Estimate` column. (It standardizes continuous predictors only — which is what you want.)
:::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Report *b* when**

- the units mean something (dollars, hours, mg)
- you want to compare predictors **within** this sample
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Report *β* when**

- the units are arbitrary (survey points)
- you want to compare **across** studies or scales
:::
:::::

. . .

Here: β = **.38** (study load) vs **.14** (sleep quality). Study load matters roughly **2.7×** as much.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## When predictors step on each other

If two predictors are nearly the same variable, the model cannot tell them apart. Coefficients get unstable and standard errors balloon.

::: callout-note
## 🖱️ Check it

**Assumption Checks → ✅ Collinearity statistics**

JAMOVI prints **VIF** and **tolerance** for each predictor.
:::

::: incremental
- Stress model: VIF = **1.004** — these predictors are strangers
- Fire model: VIF = **5.00** — acres and trucks are nearly redundant (*r* = .89), and the SE on `trucks` rose from 0.515 to 0.579 as a result
:::

. . .

Rules of thumb: \> 5 is worth a sentence, \> 10 is a problem. Note that the fire model still **worked** — high VIF widens your SEs, it does not invalidate the model.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The write-up

> Stress was regressed on self-reported study load and sleep quality in a sample of 520 students. The overall model was significant, *F*(2, 517) = 54.07, *p* \< .001, accounting for 17.3% of the variance in stress (adj. *R²* = .170). Holding sleep quality constant, each one-point increase in study load was associated with a 0.38-point increase in stress (*b* = 0.38, *SE* = 0.04, *t* = 9.54, *p* \< .001). Holding study load constant, each one-point increase in rated sleep quality was associated with a 0.17-point increase in stress (*b* = 0.17, *SE* = 0.05, *t* = 3.50, *p* \< .001). Adding sleep quality improved fit over study load alone, Δ*R²* = .020, *F*(1, 517) = 12.27, *p* \< .001. The positive coefficient for sleep quality was contrary to expectation and may reflect the direction in which that item was scored.

. . .

::: callout-tip
Everything a reader needs: the overall test, each coefficient **with its holding-constant clause**, the model comparison, and an honest flag on the odd result.
:::
